title: Effect of two-weeks endurance training wearing additional clothing in a temperate outdoor environment on performance and physiology in the heat
authors: Stevens CJ, Heathcote SL, Plews DJ, Laursen PB, Taylor L
population: 15 trained male triathletes in performance-matched groups (8 control, 7 in additional clothing)
findings: Two weeks of unsupervised cycling and running in full-length pants, a winter jacket and gloves (nylon, polyurethane, polyester) in a temperate outdoor environment was compared with training in shorts and a short-sleeve top.
Thermal sensation during the sessions was most likely hotter in the additional-clothing group (5.5 against 4.4 AU).

Tests in 32.5 C and 55% RH before and after the programme (20 min at 180 W then a 40 min self-paced time trial) showed no physiological or perceptual sign of heat acclimation, and the change in time-trial performance was trivial (-0.7%, +/- 5.4%).
The authors conclude that two weeks of training in additional clothing in a temperate environment was not an effective heat acclimation strategy for these triathletes.
limitations: Fifteen men; the sessions were unsupervised and the clothing was recorded in a diary; the clothing, the temperate weather and the length and intensity of the sessions were not controlled, so a different garment, a warmer day or a harder session could give a different result; the sessions were training for triathlon, not easy running; women were not studied. A negative result in one small study does not show that no clothing protocol can work. Abstract read on Europe PMC; the full text was not read.
implications: The only trial found on exercising overdressed as heat acclimation was negative: it is the reason the app does not count extra layers in mild weather as a heat day.
No safety finding in the abstract; heavy clothing in warm weather adds heat stress, and the cautions come from Heathcote 2018 and the consensus.

verification.notes: Added 2026-11-09 for task HT1 (rule I8). Crossref: Temperature 5:267-275, online 2018-07-03, five authors, no updated-by notice. Abstract read on Europe PMC (PMID 30377642). The same author's commentary (10.1080/23328940.2018.1437309, Temperature 5:101-102) was looked up and has no abstract, so it was not read and is not recorded. Other searches (Crossref, 2026-11-09) found no other trial of training in extra clothing or an impermeable suit as heat acclimation for runners; the protective-clothing studies found (Baumgartner 1995, Aoyagi 1998, Chang 1999) are about workers in chemical protective clothing and were not read.
